extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claim subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, including identifying statutory categories, applying judicial-exception (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) analyses for product and process claims, and sample claim analyses and rejection procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The four statutory categories of invention under 35 U.S.C. § 101 are Process, Machine, Manufacture, or Composition of Matter and improvements thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that do not fall within these categories are not eligible for patenting. Identification of one particular category is not necessary for eligibility; a claim may satisfy more than one category (e.g., bicycle may be both machine and manufacture). Analyze based on the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole. If a claim covers both eligible and ineligible subject matter, reject under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and claim-as-a-whole analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation and consider the claim as a whole in the eligibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BRI when determining whether a claim fits a statutory category and when performing judicial-exception analysis. Keep in mind what the applicant considers to be the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to claim within a statutory category → rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If, under the broadest reasonable interpretation, a claim covers an invention that does not fall within the four statutory categories, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101 must be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the claimed invention does not satisfy any of the categories (see MPEP 2106(I) for definitions). Use Form ¶¶ 7.04, 7.05, 7.05.01; use Form ¶ 7.04.01 for human organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals per se are not statutory categories (ineligible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitory, propagating signals (signals per se) are not within the four statutory categories and are therefore ineligible subject matter (In re Nuijten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under BRI, a computer readable media (CRM) may cover an ineligible signal per se unless the specification provides a special definition distinguishing storage media from transmission media. If the specification is silent, acceptable claim amendments include excluding the signal embodiment (e.g., adding 'non-transitory'), but 'non-transitory' is not required. It is not acceptable to add 'physical' or 'tangible' or to add 'storage' absent support in the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living subject matter and human organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonnaturally occurring non-human multicellular living organisms, including animals, are eligible; claims directed to or encompassing a human organism are ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2105. For human organisms, use Form ¶ 7.04.01 and applicable statutory provisions (e.g., section 33(a) of the AIA, 35 U.S.C. § 101).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have interpreted the statutory categories to exclude 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas'—the basic tools of scientific and technological work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These judicial exceptions include scientific principles, naturally occurring phenomena, mental processes, and mathematical algorithms. Other terms sometimes used include physical phenomena, scientific principles, disembodied concepts, and disembodied mathematical algorithms and formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic judicial-exception analysis (claim directed to exception or practical application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea) and whether the exception has been practically applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze all elements/steps to see if the exception is practically applied. A claim directed to a practical application may be eligible. Determine whether the claim covers all substantial applications of the exception and thereby forecloses future innovation. A claim directed solely to the exception itself is not eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-claim (machine/manufacture/composition) flowchart analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Five-step product claim analysis: (1) Does the claim meet definitions of process, machine, manufacture or composition? (2) If a process, follow process analysis. (3) Does the claim recite an abstract idea, law of nature or natural phenomenon? (4) Is the claim as a whole directed to a practical application of the exception? (5) Does the claim cover substantially all practical applications of the exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a judicial exception but is directed to a practical application (evidence: man-made tangible embodiment with a real-world use), proceed; if it covers substantially all practical applications (forecloses innovation), deem ineligible. If not drawn to an eligible subject matter, reject under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (use Form ¶¶ 7.04, 7.05, 7.05.01). See MPEP 2106(II)(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-claim analysis: laws of nature vs. abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: For process claims that include a law of nature as a limitation, use the three essential inquiries (MPEP 2106.01). For other process claims, use factors relating to abstract idea determination (including Bilski factors/Machine-or-Transformation guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate analysis path depending on whether the claim includes a natural principle limitation; see Interim Guidance for Determining Subject Matter Eligibility for Process Claims in View of Bilski v. Kappos and 2012 Interim Procedure for process claims involving laws of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three essential inquiries for laws of nature (process claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Is the claim directed to a process (an act or series of acts or steps)? 2) Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature/natural phenomenon/naturally occurring relation or correlation (i.e., is the natural principle a limiting feature)? 3) Does the claim include additional elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that it is practically applied and amount to significantly more than the natural principle itself?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask also: Is the claim more than a law of nature + the general instruction to simply 'apply it'?

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural principle as a claim limitation (definition and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural principle is the handiwork of nature and occurs without the hand of man; includes correlations that exist apart from human action (e.g., relationship between blood glucose levels and diabetes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of methods that focus on natural principles include diagnosing a condition based on naturally occurring correlations, or identifying disease using a naturally occurring relationship between a substance and disease. Claims that do not include such limitations (e.g., administering a man-made drug, treating by medical procedure, new use for a known drug) need not use this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 3 Part I – Integration evaluation (factors that weigh in favor)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether additional elements/steps integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention, consider whether: the steps relate to the natural principle in a significant way; the steps impose a meaningful limit on claim scope; the steps include a machine or transformation that implements the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that every step show integration. If additional elements/steps do not integrate the natural principle, there is no practical application and the claim fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration evaluation (factors that weigh against integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that indicate lack of integration include: the steps are insignificant extra-solution activity, or the steps are mere field-of-use restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: a claim that diagnoses by correlating a bacterium to infection and only adds 'recording the diagnosis on a chart'—the recording is extra-solution activity unrelated to the correlation and does not integrate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 3 Part II – 'Amounts to significantly more' evaluation (factors that weigh in favor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors indicating the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself: the steps do more than describe the principle with general instructions to apply it; the steps narrow claim scope so others are not foreclosed; the steps add a novel or non-obvious feature; the steps include a new use of a known substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors support finding a patent-eligible practical application of a natural principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Amounts to significantly more’ evaluation (factors that weigh against)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors weighing against the claim amounting to significantly more include: the steps are well-understood, purely conventional or routine; the steps are those that must be taken by others to apply the principle; the steps are recited at a high level of generality such that substantially all practical applications are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim amounts to no more than recognizing the law of nature (routine/high-level steps), the claim should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims – laws of nature rejection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: After conducting the three inquiries, if the claim is drawn to an ineligible law of nature/natural principle, reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form ¶¶ 7.04, 7.05, 7.05.013 and see MPEP 2106.01. Note that further examination under §§ 102, 103, and 112, and utility/double patenting may still be required for claims deemed eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims – abstract ideas determination
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that attempts to patent an abstract idea per se is ineligible; determine eligibility by weighing factors that indicate whether the claim represents a practical application of an abstract idea or the abstract idea itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factors include inquiries from the machine-or-transformation test as a useful investigative tool, but not determinative. Not every factor will be relevant; no factor is conclusive by itself; weight accorded varies with facts and technology; factors are not exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea factors that weigh toward eligibility (machine/transformation and concreteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors indicating eligibility include recitation of a machine or transformation (express or inherent) that meaningfully limits execution of steps, a particular machine or transformation implementing the steps, and an article being transformed showing a change in state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also weigh whether the claim is more than a mere statement of a concept: it describes a particular solution, implements a concept tangibly, and the performance of steps is observable and verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea factors that weigh against eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors against eligibility include no recitation of machine or transformation, or an insufficient recitation (machine is nominal, generic, merely an object, or tangential to steps). Claims that are merely statements of a general concept (cover both known and unknown uses, can be performed without apparatus) weigh against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of insufficiency: machine recited only generically covering any machine; transformations that only change position/location; 'article' is a general concept; claim only states a problem to be solved or is disembodied/imperceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of general concepts (abstract ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of example general concepts that may be abstract ideas: basic economic practices (hedging, insurance, financial transactions, marketing), basic legal theories (contracts, dispute resolution), mathematical concepts (algorithms, spatial relationships), mental activity (forming judgment, observation), interpersonal interactions, teaching concepts (memorization), human behavior (exercising, wearing clothing), instructing 'how business should be conducted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are non-exclusive examples to help identify whether a claim is directed to a general concept/abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection practice and procedural references
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is found ineligible under the analyses for product/process or judicial exceptions, reject under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the appropriate form paragraphs and cite relevant MPEP sections and interim guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use particular paragraph numbers depending on type of rejection (e.g., ¶¶ 7.04, 7.05, 7.05.011, 7.05.013, 7.05.01). Cite MPEP 2104-2111, Interim Examination Instructions (Aug 24, 2009), Bilski guidance (July 27, 2010), 2012 Interim Procedure (July 3, 2012), and cases such as In re Ferguson, In re Nuijten, Mayo v. Prometheus, and Bilski v. Kappos. Contact SPE or TQAS with questions.
